l: the sunset, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: The sunset occurs over the Atlantic beyond the Land's End, during a boat trip and as watched from nearby cliffs. The sun drops like a red round ball into the sea; after its last light disappears, the Lizard Lights burst out and an unusual green gleam appears, holding two young lovers' attention.

l: Pistol Meadow, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Pistol Meadow is a green area on the cliff path containing foreign sailors' shipwreck burial place, feared after dark because of graves and stories that other things walk there.

l: the shipwreck at Pistol Meadow, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: More than a hundred years earlier, a ship went to pieces in the cove below Pistol Meadow; over two hundred foreign sailors were buried there, while only two of seven hundred survived after the captain put them in irons.

l: the lifeboat, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_insufficient_for_rescues shipwrecks along the Cornish coast [the volunteers also use their own boats] The lifeboat is kept at the lifeboat house, whose door invites contributions and whose key is held at a nearby house and the Rectory. It is difficult to run down to the beach on a dark winter night and is not considered sufficient by itself for rescue work.

l: Cornish hedge walls, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Cornish hedge walls are stone-and-earth walls in the Lizard district, six to ten feet high and about two feet broad, dividing land instead of fences and forcing travelers along narrow, precarious tops.

l: shipwrecks along the Cornish coast, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Shipwrecks are a recurring, often deadly danger along the Cornish coast, particularly at the Lizard and its Stags rocks. In winter, wild storms or dense fogs bring wrecks almost weekly: distress guns sound, lifeboats launch, ships break apart, and notices may report “all hands lost.” The records begin with the coast’s many marked sites of destruction and John’s account of a ship vanishing within ten minutes after striking. They continue with the lighthouse attendant’s repeated winter wrecks at the Lizard, then end with John’s interest in this history and accounts from Gunwalloe, where survivors, cargo, and other wreckage reach shore.

l: Arthurian legends, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Arthurian legends are legends centered on King Arthur and associated with Cornwall, Avillion, Lyonesse, Tintagel, Camelford, and beliefs in Arthur’s return or survival in fairy land. They preserve Arthur’s existence despite time and change, while allowing competing accounts of his disappearance, burial, grave, coffin, and the Round Table. Their stories include Ygrayne, Uther Pendragon, King Mark, Tristram, and Iseult, alongside an idealized Arthur and noble knight. They unfold through a legendary region that readers may believe to differing degrees: from Arthur’s birth-place and last battle to traditions of his loss, return, and haunting of the coast. The legends portray a society where might was right and passions brought love and hate, yet sustain ideals of courage, honour, faith, chastity, devotion, service, and love of woman.

l: Kynance, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Kynance is a coastal place with a cove and rock chambers, accessible at low water, called a kitchen and drawing-room; it is valued for especially perfect natural bathing places. On the third day it cannot be visited because the tide will not suit until Wednesday or Thursday. On the fourth, it lies west along the cliff path from Lizard, visible in moonlight beyond smooth green stretches and steep, hazardous ones. By the eighth day, its waves are heard at midnight and its Devil's Throat is recalled.

l: Kennack Sands, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Kennack Sands is a solitary sandy bay on the Cornish coast, with smooth yellow sands, long Atlantic waves, rock shelters used for bathing, and water whose dangers women travelers observe while girls bathe and flowers are gathered.

l: Cadgwith, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Cadgwith is a fishing village in a sheltered coastal bend, protected from the dense fogs of the Lizard. Described as pleasant in summer and winter, it has a small fishing station, village inn, mild climate suitable for invalids, and the nearby Devil's Frying-pan as its principal attraction.

l: Mullion, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_located_in Cornwall Mullion is reached from the Lizard Down and Pradenack Down. The village contains the Old Inn, and Mullion Cove lies about a mile from it.

l: Lizard Town, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Lizard Town is a bright little town on the Lizard peninsula, with a post-office, serpentine shops, and two nearby hotels. Its commercial places provide food, drink, clothing, and ornaments. During the travelers’ excursion, they depart through it, later return toward it from Cadgwith, and on the fifth day wade in to seek a shop.

l: Poltesco, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: contains the serpentine works at Poltesco [the district's principal industrial site] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.] Poltesco contains the principal serpentine works and a pretty valley with a trout-stream and wooden bridge. The women travelers visit its show-room, see objects ranging from mantelpieces to brooches, and leave wishing they could carry away more of the workmanship.

l: the Devil's Frying-pan, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: The Devil's Frying-pan near Cadgwith is a two-acre natural amphitheatre enclosed by a high semicircular cliff. It opens to the sea through a serpentine arch, where waves reach a shingly beach amid jagged rocks and flying seabirds.

l: the serpentine works at Poltesco, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: processes serpentine [into ornamental and architectural objects] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.] The serpentine works at Poltesco employ about a dozen visible workmen and use machinery whose hum mixes with the nearby trout-stream. A workman explains the process and shows the women travelers a range of finely made serpentine goods, including vases, candlesticks, mantelpieces, tombstones, brooches, and studs.

l: the girls at Kennack Sands, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: A group of girls related to and under the narrator’s care, practical in scrambling clothing and steady-headed at Kennack Sands. On the seventh day they accompany her to Kynance Cove, bathe and are repeatedly knocked down by waves, visit the Bellows, climb Asparagus Island, avoid more dangerous rocks, return safely, and reach Lizard Point along hedge tops.

l: bathing in Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is delightful [when it is available] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.] Bathing in Cornwall is described as delightful when it can be safely done, generally at low water on a sandy floor near a comfortable cave. The women travelers do not bathe at Kennack Sands, but girls there play in the sea.

l: the Atlantic waves, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: can_sweep_bathers_off_their_feet bathers [even in calm weather] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.] The Atlantic waves at Kennack Sands are long and strong, and their recoil can take a person off their feet even in calm weather. Among the rocks and eddies, they pose a serious danger to swimmers.

l: the Cornish fishing communities, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: experience the winter hardship of the Cornish coast [with little work, fishing or market access] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.] The Cornish fishing communities are portrayed as observant but civil, with people commonly greeting and speaking to visitors. Their working people are described as honest, independent, and respectable, while the villages themselves can be quiet and isolated.

l: the serpentine industry, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is the one commerce of the district [centered at Poltesco] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.] The serpentine industry is identified as the one commerce of the district, centered at Poltesco. Its market is limited, especially in winter, when there is said to be no market for serpentine.

l: the winter hardship of the Lizard community, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: The winter hardship of the Cornish coast is seasonal unemployment: poor fishing and no market for serpentine can leave men without earnings for four months, endured through summer savings and stored hay to prevent starvation.

l: Mary Mundy, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Mary Mundy is the respected, hospitable innkeeper of the Old Inn at Mullion, a Lizard resident known for red cheeks, black eyes, and voluble, kind strong Cornish. She runs the inn, helps raise a young niece with her brother, and keeps a poem and portrait of the Scotch Professor. Away in Helstone when travelers arrive, she returns that evening, warmly feeds them, restores order, and remembers the Professor.

l: Mary Mundy's brother, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Mary Mundy’s brother is a man who helps manage the household but depends on Mary Mundy. At the Old Inn, he receives travelers during her marketing absence, regrets her absence, and struggles with household and tea arrangements while promising them tea.

l: Old Inn, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Old Inn is a praised, comfortable, full house in Mullion, associated with Mary Mundy and the Professor; travelers dine, rest, give their address, receive a warm welcome from Mary and her brother, and are served substantial homemade tea.

l: Helstone, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a town [old-fashioned market town in Cornwall] Helstone is reached after the party travels inland from Gunwalloe. The travelers rest and eat at an old-fashioned inn before finding their unknown friend, the Cornish engineer, who is well known in the town.

l: Mullion Cove, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Mullion Cove, in Cornwall, is reached by a rough road and steep descent; it has a beach, grand serpentine rocks, offshore Mullion Island, and two sea-caves visited before travelers return to the Old Inn.

l: St. Michael's Mount, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: St. Michael's Mount is a historic mount in the middle of Mount's Bay, resembling Mont St. Michel and formed by a battlemented rock, castle, chapel, mediaeval fortress, and modern residence. At its foot is a fishing village of about thirty cottages, while an underground tiny continuous-chain railway serves the Mount. By moonlight it appears grand and mysterious, linked to Cormoran as his legendary dwelling place. The St. Aubyn family bought it in 1660 and has inhabited it ever since. Visitors tour its chapel, vault, halls, drawing-room, and school-room, admiring the site despite its many steps, rough causeway, and difficulties of living there. It receives royal visitors, including an expected visit by Princess Frederica of Hanover and Baron Von Pawel-Rammingen, and shines in the setting sun as travelers pass nearby.

l: Dozmare Pool, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Dozmare Pool, near St. Neots, is proposed as the mere of King Arthur’s final departure after his death-wound. Though the travelers do not visit it, they imagine a melancholy, ghostly moorland lake, associated in Cornish ghost stories with Tregeagle, spectral hounds, a phantom coach, and unexplained lights.

l: the narrator, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: The narrator, a mother of six children, travels with girls around the Lizard and Kynance Cove. She balances curiosity and affection with caution: at the Bellows and Asparagus Island she distinguishes sensible bravery from foolhardy risk, warns the girls away from Hell’s Mouth, and leaves before the tide blocks the route. Walking to Lizard Point, she receives news of sickness and death but finds consolation in moonlight. On her final day she is sad to leave, anxious over Church Cove’s slippery rocks, joins a boat trip and cave visit, hears John’s wreck account, and departs grateful for local kindness and companionship.

l: Excalibur, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Excalibur is King Arthur’s sword. Near the end of Arthur’s life, Arthur orders Sir Bedevere to throw it into a mere, said to be Dozmare Pool; its return there is associated with Arthur’s final departure.

l: the sea-caves, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Mullion Cove has two sea-caves: one on the beach and an outer cave accessible only at low water. The narrator passes through the near cave's dark, winding, seaweed-damp passage and emerges into a secluded sandy nook.

l: the tide, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_rising fast [at Mullion Cove] The tide is rising fast while visitors are in the farther cave. Several people have to wade ashore up to their knees, and the narrator realizes that she and her companions must hurry or wade through the water themselves.

l: Mullion Cove's serpentine rocks, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: are_made_of serpentine [grand enclosing rocks] Mullion Cove's grand serpentine rocks enclose the beach and the secluded nook beyond the cave. The rocks form walls around the nook and are also used for serpentine candlesticks at the Old Inn.

l: the tea at the Old Inn, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Mary Mundy serves the travelers a substantial tea with hot strong tea, a large home-baked loaf, rich yellow butter, cream, clotted cream, jam, and marmalade. She repeatedly urges them to have more and charges little for the meal.

l: Landewednack, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Landewednack is a parish containing the comparatively modern Lizard Town. On the journey’s fourth day it is the narrator’s destination for an afternoon church visit; its name is said to mean the white-roofed church of St. Wednack in ancient Cornish. By the fifth day it prepares for a harvest festival, with ticketed tea in the rectory garden and an evening thanksgiving service. Its rectors reportedly included one who died aged 120 in 1683.

l: the church of Landewednack, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: The church of Landewednack, near Lizard Town and close to the sea, is described as England’s most southerly church. Picturesque and carefully maintained, it combines older features, a Norman doorway and curious hagioscope, with a modern serpentine memorial pulpit and neat churchyard. On the fourth day of travel it is noted for its history and notably good choir; by the sixth, the crowded evening service, beautiful music, and rich flowers and fruit make an especially impressive conclusion.

l: the Lizard storm, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: The Lizard storm is an especially awful Cornwall storm of torrential rain and howling wind. Beginning on the fourth day after clear, silent skies, it brings an extraordinary deluge and shrieking wind, convincing the narrator that the weather has broken.

l: the harvest festival, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: includes the evening thanksgiving service [after tea in the rectory garden] The harvest festival is scheduled for the day after the storm and includes tea in the rectory garden followed by an evening thanksgiving service. The text questions how thankful the festival can seem to farmers after such damaging weather.

l: Sunday, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Sunday is a day of rest, Sabbatic peace, and rejoicing. It unfolds first in calm beauty: a cliff walk, morning churchgoing, sunset, and moonlit scenery, before a night storm sharply changes the mood. Later, quiet roads near Land’s End are nearly empty as local people go to church or school; despite guilt about traveling during church hours, the narrator finds deep peace and believes Sunday can be kept outside church doors.

l: the storm, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: The storm begins at night, obscuring the sea with torrential rain. On the fourth day, rain and wind turn sea and sky into indistinguishable blackness, hiding moon and stars, and continue until dawn. On the fifth day it gradually abates; by sunset wind and rain stop, though flooded lanes and an angry sea remain.

l: the evening church service, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: The evening church service fills every seat, with chanting, hymns, a harvest anthem, organ music, expressive prayers, a good sermon, and a brilliant closing voluntary.

l: the holiday in Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_affected_by the Lizard storm [the weather breaks after four days] The holiday in Cornwall has lasted only four days when the weather breaks. The narrator laments that the storm may spoil the holiday, as well as the planned harvest festival.

l: the fire, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a fire [the first fire of the season] The travelers decide that they must have a fire, which requires removing their sea-holly and ferns and causes concern for their handmaiden. After initially filling the room with smoke, the fire burns properly and makes the room warm, bright, and comfortable.

l: the rain, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a down-pour [even and very heavy] The rain falls heavily throughout most of the day, making the road to Lizard Town literally swimable and leaving the travelers wading through it. It abates somewhat in the afternoon and ceases by sunset.

l: Housel Cove, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Housel Cove is an Atlantic-coast cove and secluded bathing place with soft sand and a beautiful serpentine-rock dressing-room. On the sixth day, the narrator and companions spend a divine morning bathing there without organized amusement. On the eighth day, the women return through the fields and again find the bathing delightful.

l: Idylls of the King, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: contains The Passing of Arthur [as its concluding section] The travelers read the Idylls of the King all the way through, ending with The Passing of Arthur. Its account of Sir Bedivere throwing Excalibur into the mere deeply moves one of the travelers and prompts a debate about ideals and belief.

l: the ideal man, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_impossible ideal [as a conception] The travelers discuss whether it is better to believe in an impossible ideal man than to accept and worship a worldly, mean, or base ideal. The question leads to a long and heated argument.

l: Cornish coast-life, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Cornish coast-life in winter commonly brings rain, storms, and fogs, with little frost or snow; a storm during the journey shows the travelers what this life is like throughout the season.

l: Lizard Point, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a grand rock Lizard Point is a grand rock reached by the girls through a route mainly along the tops of hedges. The narrator and the girls walk there in the evening and watch a fine sunset.

l: the laws of the universe, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: must_be_carried_out at any cost [even to individuals or nations] The laws of the universe must be carried out, even when doing so causes suffering to individuals or nations. Their operation remains connected with mysteries that the text says are not explained.

l: the mystery of sorrow, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: remains forever unexplained The mystery of sorrow, like the greater mystery of evil, remains unexplained. The text nevertheless affirms that the world can be made marvelously beautiful despite sorrow and even after a day when it seems hardly worth living in.

l: DAY THE SIXTH, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: DAY THE SIXTH is a perfect autumn morning and day, cloudless and calm, spent bathing, sketching, attending rectory tea and church, then walking beneath moonlight.

l: the rectory tea, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: brings_together rich and poor [for courtesy rather than charity] The rectory tea brings together humble parishioners, elderly people, county families, and other guests. It takes place in a flower-filled garden with tea tables, lawn-tennis on sea-sand, and music from the village wind band before the congregation goes to church.

l: the village wind band, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: The village wind band, about six wind instruments played by village musicians, performs determinedly flat with a loud, irregular bass. Compared aspirationally with the Philharmonic and Crystal Palace orchestra, it plays at the rectory tea and near hotels, drives listeners away, and ends with “God save the Queen.”

l: the elderly clergyman, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: An elderly, expressive clergyman and father who values reasonable activity but despises foolhardy bravado. On the sands, he warns two young people away from a dangerous route near Devil's Throat, notes that his daughters are safely climbing Asparagus Rock, discusses his views with the narrator, and becomes a friendly companion for a time.

l: Drawing-room Cave, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a cave [the loveliest at Kynance] The Drawing-room Cave is described as the loveliest of the caves at Kynance Cove, with a floor of soft sand. The narrator and the girls retreat there after bathing, but waves soon begin to cover its floor as the tide comes in.

l: the Bellows, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a rock fissure [producing a spout and roar in certain tide conditions] The Bellows is a curious feature at Kynance Cove where, under certain tidal conditions, water forces itself through a narrow fissure in the rock with a loud roar. The narrator visits it with the girls and watches for the largest spout.

l: Devil's Throat, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Devil's Throat, also called Hell's Mouth, is a dangerous rock passage requiring a jump over boiling waves. John Curgenven identifies it as a place visitors should not attempt; despite an elderly clergyman's warning, two young people crawl toward its fissure and cave.

l: Hell's Mouth, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_dangerous dangerous rock passage Hell's Mouth is another name given for the dangerous place John Curgenven warns the party not to attempt. The narrator repeats his warning to the girls and is relieved that they do not try it.

l: the narrator and traveling party, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: A traveling party on a Cornish tour, accompanied by Charles as carriage driver, moves through the Lizard, Marazion, Penzance, St. Ives, Land's End, and Whitesand Bay. Their chief goal is Land's End, a lifelong desire reached on a quiet Sunday after travel from Penzance and a visit to the Logan Rock. Before that, they spend their last Lizard day bathing, observing a solar rainbow, touring the Lizard Lights, and hearing wreck accounts; they also take an open-boat bath near Marazion and visit St. Michael's Mount. They admire scenery and associations but dislike Marazion's beach and St. Ives. At Land's End they explore cliffs with a sailor guide and hear local stories. Preferring terra firma to a mine, they return to Whitesand Bay for shell collecting, revisit Land's End, return to Penzance, and arrange departure.

l: the tide, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: The tide comes in quickly at Kynance Cove, covering the sandy floor of Drawing-room Cave by noon and turning a visitor’s rock into an island. The narrator’s party leaves before the route is impassable, while newly arrived tourists are isolated and may need to wade or swim ashore.

l: Penolver, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a headland [fine and green] Penolver appears as a fine headland near Housel Cove. The clerical friend's daughters climb over it, and the young folks later go there for a scramble.

l: Marazion, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Marazion is a quiet town opposite St. Michael's Mount, reached from its shore, with a name linked to Mara-Zion, Jewish colonists, and Phoenician tin trading. Chosen as the women's next resting-place for its history, position, and promised comfort, it first appears after a gorgeous sunset as a picturesque-named but extremely commonplace little town. Its warm welcome and comfortable, home-like old-fashioned inn secure their stay. Though a mild little station, it proves unsuitable for bathing: the small beach is ugly, fishy-smelling, crowded, and covered by dirty shallow water. After visiting the Mount, the travelers leave for St. Ives. Later, the town gathers at beach and station for Princess Frederica of Hanover's expected arrival, watching boats head toward the Mount and speculating about the party.

l: Penzance, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Penzance is a genteel, extremely civilised town in Cornwall, connected to Falmouth by a good but lonely road. Travelers pass through, preferring Marazion because Penzance seems too genteel despite lovely, richly vegetated surroundings and coastal views. They later return in the evening to arrange departure, discuss a Marazion house, and prepare Charles’s drive to Falmouth.

l: Church Cove, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a cove [landing place for the boat trip] Church Cove is reached after the travelers leave their carriage, and they descend to the shore to board John's boat. Its rough, slippery rocks and advancing waves make both embarkation and landing difficult.

l: the clerical friend of Kynance, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: The clerical friend tells the women that his children have bathed near Kynance, walked to Cadgwith, and gone launce-fishing by moonlight. He explains how launce-fishing is performed and says his children returned home about two o'clock in the morning.

l: the lighthouse attendant, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: A young, intelligent lighthouse attendant of working-man status, sickly-faced and coughing, guides women through the Lizard Lights, explains its instruments, and recounts wrecks he has witnessed during their limited visit.

l: Sir Launcelot, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a bravest knight of King Arthur [and dearest friend] Sir Launcelot is described as King Arthur’s bravest knight and dearest friend. He is the man for whose love Queen Guinevere forsakes Arthur.

l: launce-fishing, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a sport [a popular Lizard pastime practiced on moonlight nights] Launce-fishing is described as a popular Lizard pastime carried out on moonlit nights. Participants stand barefoot on wet sand, use a crooked iron spear to hook sand-eels, and may cook their catch over a fire around midnight.

l: the launce, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: The launce is a sand-eel peculiar to the Cornish coasts. It swims during the day, then at night burrows in sand above the waterline, where moonlight reveals its silvery gleam.

l: the perfect solar rainbow, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a luminous circle around the sun [with faint prismatic tints and extending over half the sky] The women see a rare perfect solar rainbow after bathing at Housel Cove. It forms a luminous circle around the sun, changes from yellow to faint prismatic colors, and gradually disappears.

l: the lighthouse built by the Cornish engineer, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: produces light [nightly, equal to about 30,000 candles] The lighthouse at the Lizard is represented by the huge white building containing the enormous light and fog-horn apparatus. Its purpose is to help save ships and lives along a dangerous coast.

l: the lighthouse machinery, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: operates the fog-horn [through complicated mechanisms] The lighthouse machinery includes Brobdingnagian lamps, devices for producing the light, and complicated mechanisms for keeping the fog-horn working when the light becomes invisible. The light is said to equal about 30,000 candles.

l: the planned boat excursion to the sea-caves, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: A planned boat excursion to the sea-caves is proposed after earlier boating plans with John Curgenven fail. With little time left at the Lizard, Charles suggests taking a boat from Church Cove before the party drives onward, and the women agree. The voyage unfolds in small open boats on rough, hazardous water, amid heavy waves, rocks, cliffs, and open sea. John rows confidently and takes the party into Raven's Ugo and Dolor Ugo, where they admire the caves and hear of wrecks and smugglers. In another rough-water passage from Porth Hern, two boatmen guide the party past cliffs and a slate quarry into a dark cave; fear and awe give way to daylight and sunshine on the return.

l: the journey to Marazion, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: The women plan to leave at 10 A.M. for Marazion by way of Helstone, where they hope to stay for an hour or two. After Charles's proposal, they plan to start at nine, visit the sea-caves, reach Helstone by dinner-time, and arrive at Marazion before dark.

l: death, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a friend [for the old and spiritually prepared] The narrator reflects that death appears differently to the old, who may see it not as an enemy but as a friend. She imagines death as unable to harm them and possibly able to restore what life has denied or taken away.

l: the afterlife, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a eternal life [believed to be a possible blessing beyond death] The narrator considers the possibility that something within people is imperishable even as the body declines. She expresses faith that death may lead to the Father's care and that more and better things may be given after this life.

l: the Cornish engineer, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: The Cornish engineer is a clever, highly reliable mechanical engineer whose conscientiousness, probity, and fidelity are valued by employers and by the family he once served abroad. Young in Brazil, he worked for a gold-mining company, later superintended engineering projects, and built a lighthouse with sole charge. In later life he warmly welcomes the narrator’s party, displays inventions, preserves the Emperor’s candle as a relic, and offers hospitality.

l: Raven's Ugo, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Raven's Ugo is a sea cave, first examined by a party from a boat on their last day at the Lizard. Above the sea line and hung with sea-ferns, its entrance is occupied by a pair of ravens; formerly, smugglers hid kegs of spirits there.

l: Dolor Ugo, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Dolor Ugo is an inaccessible, unusable sea cave, solemn and colorful, with a floor entirely of clear, deep olive-green heaving water. Boats can enter only to the daylight’s reach; beyond that, its extent remains unknown because exploration would require dangerous swimming.

l: the Lizard coast, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a iron-bound coast [marked by great gloomy cliffs] The Lizard coast is portrayed as magnificent, gloomy, and iron-bound, with cliffs, sea caves, and a history of wrecks and smuggling. The narrator regrets that the party's boat trip provides its last view of the coast.

l: the emigrant ship Brest, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: was_lost_in shipwrecks on the Lizard coast [during a winter night] The Brest went down near the Lizard on a winter night. Its survivors included women and children who were rescued in boats, brought ashore with little clothing, and sheltered by fishermen's cottages and the parsonage.

l: the journey from the Lizard to Helstone, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a inland carriage journey [over bleak and beautiful country] The journey includes the return from Church Cove, drying wet clothes, visits to Mary Mundy, Mullion, and Gunwalloe, and a long inland drive through quiet villages and apple-growing country. The travelers eventually reach Helstone, where they rest and visit the Cornish engineer.

l: the landing at Church Cove, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: has_condition slippery sea-weedy rocks [between advancing waves] Landing at Church Cove requires a leap from the boat onto slippery, seaweed-covered rocks between the waves. The narrator watches her children land first and is relieved when she herself reaches firm ground.

l: Cornish hospitality, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Cornish hospitality is shown on the Lizard through fishermen rescuing and sheltering Brest survivors, a laundress warming travelers, an apple seller's generosity, and a Helstone couple's lavish tea and fruit. Beginning as a mere map dot, the Lizard gains living human interest through repeated help whose givers often refuse payment or thanks.

l: personal fidelity, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a passionate personal loyalty [shown by the Cornish engineer toward his former employers' family] Personal fidelity is embodied by the Cornish engineer's lasting devotion to the family of those who employed him. He preserves their likenesses, remembers their kindness, keeps the emperor's lighthouse-lighting candle, and declares that he would travel anywhere to serve them.

l: Loe Pool, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Loe Pool is a small lake near Helstone, separated from the sea by a sandbar. Supposedly formed by Tregeagle, it is periodically ceremonially cut through by the Mayor of Helstone so fresh and salt waters meet; travelers discussed but did not visit it.

l: moonlit row around St. Michael's Mount, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a row [at night, in moonlight] The travelers undertake a moonlit row around St. Michael's Mount after Charles suggests it. The mild air and shimmering water transform the ordinary town and the Mount into a dreamlike, almost fairy-tale scene, allowing the travelers to imagine the area's legends and history.

l: St. Ives, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: St. Ives is a town with dark, narrow, fish-smelling streets, a pilchard fishery, a Town Hall, and Tregenna, an ancient mansion made into an hotel. Travelers reach it by a beautiful but inconvenient road, dislike it and its meal, are shown around by a friendly elderly local man, and hurry back toward Penzance.

l: Queen Guinevere, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Queen Guinevere, daughter of King Leodegrance and wife of King Arthur, loves Sir Launcelot to the detriment of her marriage. She forsakes Arthur for Launcelot; tradition says her body was found with Arthur’s at Winchester.

l: Sennen, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Sennen is a pretty village with cottages, lodgings, a new schoolhouse, and the ancient parish church St. Sennen's. It is linked to a long-deceased curate whose son the traveling party meets at Land's End. After seeing lights on St. Sennen's in darkness, the party passes through the village in heavy rain; the narrator then encounters local residents and schoolchildren, highlighting schooling amid illiteracy.

l: the Logan Rock, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: The Logan Rock is a massive rocking stone near Treryn, regarded as England’s most remarkable specimen and celebrated since the narrator’s childhood. In 1824 Lieutenant Goldsmith displaced it and was forced to replace it. Though visitors later seek its motion with a guide, it no longer rocks properly.

l: the guide, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: A solemn Cornish-born sailor-guide, formerly a man-of-war’s-man, leads visitors across fields to the Logan Rock and safely along Land’s End’s perilous rocks. He recounts shipwrecks, Royal Navy service aboard H.M.S. Agamemnon, and Balaklava, then gives the narrator a glittering stone.

l: Whitesand Bay, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Whitesand Bay is a wide, sunny sweep of fine sand with minute, varied shells, bright sea, and shallow-looking water. Revisited on a clear Monday for bazaar shells, it delights companions, though an old woman warns bathing may be unsafe from quicksands.

l: the Land's End journey, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a fulfilled lifelong desire [with no disappointment in the reality] The Land's End journey fulfills a wish the narrator and traveling party have held for many years. They see the Logan Rock and the cliffs, meet local people, and experience the grandeur of the coast, though rain prevents them from fully visiting Whitesand Bay and other planned sights.

l: Botallack Mine, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a Cornish mine Botallack Mine is one of several places the narrator and her companions are told they must see, especially by those with scientific interests. They decide not to visit it, partly because they prefer the coast and partly because they do not wish to descend into a mine.

l: shell collecting, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a fascination [for the travellers] The companions collect very small shells at Whitesand Bay, some no larger than a grain of rice or a pin's head. The narrator considers the beach's shells exceptionally beautiful and becomes more absorbed in their delicate perfection than in the historical figures associated with the coast.

l: Princess Frederica of Hanover, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Princess Frederica of Hanover, a young half-English, half-foreign princess, marries her father’s secretary, Baron Von Pawel-Rammingen; public fascination follows their romance, then sadness after their infant’s funeral, before their expected visit to St. Michael’s Mount.

l: the royal visit to St. Michael's Mount, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_hosted_by the St. Aubyns [as a visit to their residence] The royal visit draws much of Marazion to the beach and leads people to follow the visitors' boats at a respectful distance. The crowd speculates about which person is the princess, how the St. Aubyns will receive the party, and whether the visitors will tour Land's End.

l: the journey from Penzance to Falmouth, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a long and lonely drive [undertaken at night] The journey from Penzance to Falmouth is planned for the middle of the night, after the horse has rested. Charles expects the road to be good but lonely, and intends to use the old moon after one o'clock to reach Falmouth by daylight.

l: Tintagel, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Tintagel is a natural-artificial fortress on a rocky sea promontory, identified as King Arthur’s legendary birthplace and as a castle associated with Ygrayne and the duke of Cornwall. It is also presented as the home of King Mark, Sir Tristram, and Iseult of Ireland. Approached through lonely country, its black rock and surrounding sea are seen at sunset. Travelers visit its decaying ruins, climb its rocks, and find a chapel and spring atop the rock, experiencing a place poised between legend and recorded history.

l: Camelford, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Camelford is a respectable, commonplace little town with shops, an inn, and private houses. It is chiefly associated in legend with King Arthur’s last battle, though it is not presented as Camelot. Travelers pass from the town to the River Camel and Slaughter Bridge, said to mark Arthur’s army’s defeat and his death-wound.

l: King Uther Pendragon, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: King Uther Pendragon is king of Britain. He falls in love with Ygrayne, besieges her and her husband in Tintagel and Terrabil, has her husband killed, and marries her. After Uther’s death, their son Arthur is proclaimed king in his stead.

l: Ygrayne, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Ygrayne, a hapless woman in the Arthurian legends, is first the duke of Cornwall’s wife. King Uther Pendragon falls in love with her; after her husband is slain, she marries Uther, bears Arthur, and later recognizes him when he is proclaimed king.

l: the Order of Knights of the Round Table, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a order of knights [dedicated to punishing vice and rescuing oppressed virtue] The Order of Knights of the Round Table is instituted by King Arthur. Its members are expected to travel everywhere, punish vice, and rescue oppressed virtue for the love of God and a noble lady.

l: Knights of the Round Table, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: The Knights of the Round Table serve as Arthur’s order of wandering defenders. One by one, Arthur’s best knights are said to fall away into sin.

l: Mordred, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Mordred, King Arthur’s nephew, raises a rebellion against Arthur, fights him at Camelford, and conquers him.

l: the Round Table, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: The Round Table is associated with the order of knights instituted by King Arthur. The text says that the Round Table, like Arthur’s coffin, is preserved at Winchester.

l: Delabole quarries, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Delabole quarries are a stark industrial world of enormous slate masses and debris heaps, worked since Queen Elizabeth’s time. In the region of Tintagel and Camelford, wagons, horses, and steam engines sustain wholesome labor, producing slate for nearby houses, walls, gates, and fences.

l: Trevena, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a village [small and quiet despite tourists] Trevena is described as a small village with one street, two inns, and a picturesque old post-office. Despite the increasing number of tourists, it retains a simple and home-like character.

l: Tintagel Castle, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Tintagel Castle is a landmark between legend and actual history, made of two castles, one in the sea and one on mainland heights, joined by a narrow causeway. In the travelers’ first view, its steep, dangerous appearance in fast-coming twilight keeps them on nearby cliffs and fields. Its ruins include a prehistoric-looking bastion and gateway, later remains, a spring, chapel, and small burial-ground. Its history is uncertain, possibly linked to Arthur, King Mark, or Castle Terrabil, while winds, waves, and the sea continually erode and divide it.

l: the sunset at Tintagel, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: The sunset at Tintagel unfolds over black foreground rock and the sea covering vanished Lyonesse beneath an amber sky barred with long clouds. A low boat-shaped cloud seems to carry three figures, imagined as King Arthur and the three queens, before the travelers joke that the dark shape at its bow is Arthur’s luggage.

l: Bossinney Cove, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Bossinney Cove is a pleasant, shut-in cove, visited three times daily by an old sand-collecting man and his eleven named donkeys. During Arthurian days, the narrator and companions bathe there, remembering its steep dangerous path, secluded water, and patient man and animals.

l: Boscastle, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a village [built at the end of a deep narrow creek] Boscastle is described as a picturesque village at the end of a deep, narrow creek that shelters sizable vessels. Its surroundings include headlands, the remains of Bottrieux Castle, Ferrabury Church, a blow-hole, and a legend about church bells lost at sea.

l: Porth Hern, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Porth Hern, the iron gate opposite Tintagel, receives a rocky stream from Trevena; across Arthurian days, the narrator and companions depart there by boat to visit sea-caves beyond Tintagel.

l: sea-cave beyond Tintagel, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: A dark, narrow, dangerous sea-cave beyond Tintagel, reached by boat from Porth Hern through stormy water and towering cliffs; its confined waves and tunnel-like darkness inspire terror and intense beauty, ending in the narrator’s vivid but incomplete memory.

l: Arthurian chivalry, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: Arthurian chivalry is an ideal that begins by enjoining courage, honour, and chivalrous love of woman, and unfolds as faith, chastity, worship of God, service to humanity, reverence for women, conscience, redressing wrongs, avoiding slander, and fidelity.

l: L'ENVOI, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_published_in London L'ENVOI Written more than a year after.] L'ENVOI was written more than a year after the events described. It concludes the history of the journey and is followed by the statement "THE END."

l: history of the fifteen innocent days, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: A history of the fifteen innocent days, ending in December fog after recounting the group's calm, bright journey through Cornwall.

l: the fifteen innocent days, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: The fifteen innocent days were calm and bright, unfolding as we three took an Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall.

l: a good time, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
s: is_a memorial [simple] L'ENVOI Written more than a year after.] "A good time" is how Americans would call the experience memorialized by the writer. Its sunshine may cast brightness far forward, even into the quiet time "when travelling days are done."

q: Step by step Dr. Inglis fought for the students.

s: University of Edinburgh admits women doctors (to examinations for degrees in medicine)
q: When the University of Edinburgh admitted women to the examinations for degrees in medicine, Dr. Inglis graduated M.B., C.M. in 1899.

s: University of Edinburgh opens its doors to women doctors (under a new Head)
q: She had achieved many things, and was far away from her city and its hard-earned practice when at length, in 1916, the University, under a new ‘open-minded, generous-hearted Head,’ opened its doors to women medical students.

s: Elsie Inglis serves on Central Edinburgh Women’s Liberal Association (as Vice-President)
q: She joined the Central Edinburgh Women’s Liberal Association in its earliest organised years. She acted as Vice-President in it for sixteen years, and was one of its most active members.

s: Elsie Inglis leaves the Liberal Party (to advance women’s causes independently)
q: It was not until she became convinced that she could help forward the great cause for women better by being unattached to any party organisation that she severed her connection with the Liberal Party.

s: Elsie Inglis serves on Women’s Liberal League (as a founding committee member)
q: In 1901 she was a member of the Women’s Liberal League, a branch of the W.L.A. which split off at the time of the Boer War, in opposition to the ‘Little Englanders.’ Dr. Inglis was on its first committee, and lent her drawing-room for meetings, addressing other meetings on the Imperialist doctrines born in that war.

s: Elsie Inglis practises in Edinburgh (after qualifying in medicine)
q: Elsie Inglis took up practice in Edinburgh, and worked in a happy partnership with the late Dr. Jessie MacGregor, until the latter left Scotland for work in America.

s: Elsie Inglis founds Muir Hall of Residence for Women Students (for women students at the University)
q: Among her other enterprises was the founding of the Muir Hall of Residence for Women Students at the University.

s: Elsie Inglis serves as honorary secretary of Muir Hall of Residence for Women Students (until her death)
q: Dr. Inglis was Hon. Secretary to the Muir Hall till she died, and from its start was a moving spirit in all that stood for the comfort of the students.

s: Elsie Inglis founds Hospice in the High Street of Edinburgh (as a maternity and infant-welfare centre)
q: Thus the Hospice in the High Street was opened in 1904. Dr. Inglis devoted herself to the work.

s: Hospice in the High Street of Edinburgh trains nurses (for the C.M.B. examination)
q: The midwifery department grew so rapidly that after a few years the Hospice became a centre, one of five in Scotland, for training nurses for the C.M.B. examination.

s: Hospice in the High Street of Edinburgh provides medical education (opportunities unavailable in other maternity hospitals)
q: This affords women students opportunities denied to them in other maternity hospitals.

s: Elsie Inglis amalgamates Hospice in the High Street of Edinburgh (with Bruntsfield Hospital)
q: In that year the Hospice was amalgamated with Bruntsfield Hospital; medical, surgical, and gynecological cases were treated there, while the Hospice was devoted entirely to maternity and infant welfare cases.

s: Bruntsfield Hospital treats medical practice (medical, surgical, and gynecological cases)
q: In that year the Hospice was amalgamated with Bruntsfield Hospital; medical, surgical, and gynecological cases were treated there, while the Hospice was devoted entirely to maternity and infant welfare cases.

s: Hospice in the High Street of Edinburgh grew out of a nursing home for working women (near their own homes)
q: The Hospice grew out of the establishment of a nursing home for working women, where they could be cared for near their own homes.

s: Elsie Inglis develops surgical skill (while serving abroad under wartime pressure)
q: When in the Scottish Women’s Hospitals abroad, Dr. Inglis rapidly acquired a surgical skill, under the tremendous pressure of work, which often kept her for days at the operating-table, which showed what a great surgeon she might have been, given equal advantages in the days of her peace practice.

s: Elsie Inglis partners with Dr. Jessie MacGregor (in medical practice)
q: Elsie Inglis took up practice in Edinburgh, and worked in a happy partnership with the late Dr. Jessie MacGregor, until the latter left Scotland for work in America.

s: Elsie Inglis serves patients and local families (without charging some families fees)
q: She would never take any fees from this family.

s: Elsie Inglis oversees dispensary of St. Anne (for the Little Sisters of the Poor)
q: The Little Sisters of the Poor had a dispensary of St. Anne, and Dr. Elsie had it in her charge from 1903 to 1913, and the Sister Superior speaks of the affection of the people and the good work done among them.

s: Elsie Inglis serves St. Cuthbert’s Mission (as a physician three mornings a week)
q: The caretaker of the dispensary in St. Cuthbert’s Mission in Morrison Street speaks of Dr. Inglis as the true friend of all who needed her. She gave an hour three mornings in the week, and if she could not overtake all the cases in the time, she would occasionally come back later in the day.

s: Elsie Inglis is remembered by patients and local families (for medical, practical, and personal kindness)
q: These were the true mourners who stood round St. Giles’ with the bairns she had ‘brought home’ on the day when her earthly presence passed from their sight.

s: Elsie Inglis is a medical practitioner (with a strong and directive manner)
q: The husband said she was so bright one felt the better for her visit, ‘though her orders had to be obeyed and no mistake, and she would tell you off at once if you did not carry them out.’

s: Elsie Inglis graduates from University of Edinburgh (with M.B., C.M.)
q: When the University of Edinburgh admitted women to the examinations for degrees in medicine, Dr. Inglis graduated M.B., C.M. in 1899.

s: Elsie Inglis loses John Inglis (through his death)
q: Her father’s death deprived her of what had been the very centre and mainspring of her existence.

s: Elsie Inglis practises at Atholl Place (with Dr. Jessie MacGregor)
q: The two doctors started practice in Atholl Place, and later on they moved into 8 Walker Street, an abode which will always be associated with the name of Dr. Elsie Inglis.

s: Elsie Inglis resides at 8 Walker Street (with Dr. Jessie MacGregor)
q: The two doctors started practice in Atholl Place, and later on they moved into 8 Walker Street, an abode which will always be associated with the name of Dr. Elsie Inglis.

s: Elsie Inglis lectures at Medical College for Women (on Gynecology)
q: She was a lecturer on Gynecology in the Medical College for Women which had been started later than Dr. Jex Blake’s school, and was on slightly broader lines.

s: Elsie Inglis is a medical practitioner (in Edinburgh)
q: Dr. Elsie’s power of sympathy and understanding was as much called upon in her paying practice as among the very poor.

s: Elsie Inglis takes recreation in September (as her annual month of recreation)
q: She always had September as her month of recreation.

s: Elsie Inglis takes solitary holidays out-of-the-way places (for a fortnight before rejoining her family)
q: She used to go away, first of all, for a fortnight quite alone to some out-of-the-way place, when not even her letters were sent after her.

s: Elsie Inglis requires hot water (for baths when choosing holiday accommodation)
q: Her first requirement was hot water for ‘baths.’

s: Elsie Inglis travels with paintbox (during holidays)
q: Her paintbox went with her

s: Elsie Inglis maintains self-command (in adverse circumstances and professional crises)
q: Those who were with her in the ‘retreats’ in Serbia or Russia saw the same quality of self-command.

s: Elsie Inglis uses family prayers (before breakfast, regardless of late-night work)
q: However late she came downstairs after any night-work, there was always family prayers before breakfast.

s: Elsie Inglis uses Euchologion (as her prayer book)
q: The book she used was _Euchologion_, and when in Russia asked that a copy should be sent her.

s: Elsie Inglis possesses Elsie Inglis's father's books (kept in her consulting-room)
q: Her consulting-room was lined with bookshelves containing all her father’s books, and of these she never lost sight.

s: Elsie Inglis supports women as citizens or as doctors (through increasingly particular dress and uniform)
q: In her dress she became increasingly particular, but only as the adornment, not of herself, but of the cause of women as citizens or as doctors.
